# Response to selection: the other half of the objective {#sec-response} Every chapter so far measures what selection *spends*. None of them writes down what it *buys*. That asymmetry is not cosmetic. @sec-cycles will show a constrained programme overtaking an unconstrained one after several cycles, at a crossover cycle that varies with the simulation seed, and the book can report that because it simulated it -- not because anything in the preceding chapters predicts it. A reader who wants to know when the crossover arrives in *their* programme has no way to find out except to re-run the simulation with their own parameters. The quantitative genetics that answers such questions is older than any of the genomic machinery here, and this chapter installs it: the variance selection acts on, the equation that turns that variance into gain, and the classical index theory that turns out to be the direct ancestor of this book's $\alpha$ constraint. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sim <- simulate_pools(n_A = book_cfg$n_pool_A, n_B = book_cfg$n_pool_B, m = book_cfg$m, fst = 0.15, n_qtl = 300, h2 = 0.5, seed = 1) X <- sim$X # N x m hybrids, 0/0.5/1 gv <- drop(X %*% sim$beta) # true genetic value, known here by construction I <- sim$index # what the breeder actually sees c(hybrids = nrow(X), markers = ncol(X), qtl = sum(sim$beta != 0)) #> hybrids markers qtl #> 625 2000 300 ``` ::: ## The breeder's equation, and how well it does here Response to one round of truncation selection is $$R \;=\; i \, r \, \sigma_A$$ {#eq-response-breeders} with $i$ the selection intensity (a property of the selected fraction alone), $r$ the accuracy of the criterion as a predictor of genetic value, and $\sigma_A$ the additive standard deviation [@falconer1996, ch. 11]. Here the genetic value of the hybrids is the vector $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta$ (`gv`), purely additive in the marker coding by construction of `simulate_pools()`, so $\sigma_A$ is estimated by `sd(gv)`. `sel_intensity()` returns $i$; later chapters use it inside the usefulness criterion (@sec-stages) and in a replicated check of this equation (@sec-alphasimr). @tbl-response-breeders sets the predicted response of @eq-response-breeders beside the realised one for the top 60 hybrids on the index. ::: {#tbl-response-breeders .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='One round of truncation selection of the top 60 of the 625 hybrids on the index (`simulate_pools()`, 25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, 300 QTL, $h^2 = 0.5$, $F_{ST} = 0.15$, seed 1). $i$: normal-theory selection intensity of the selected fraction; $r$: correlation between index and true genetic value; $\sigma_A$: standard deviation of the true genetic value; predicted: $i\,r\,\sigma_A$ (@eq-response-breeders); realised: mean genetic value of the selected minus that of all hybrids. Genetic values in simulation units.'} ```{.r .cell-code} n_sel <- 60 N <- nrow(X) i_norm <- sel_intensity(n_sel / N) r <- cor(I, gv) sel <- order(I, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)] fmt(data.frame(`intensity i` = i_norm, `accuracy r` = r, `additive s.d. (sim. units)` = sd(gv), `predicted response (sim. units)` = i_norm * r * sd(gv), `realised response (sim. units)` = mean(gv[sel]) - mean(gv), check.names = FALSE), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| intensity i| accuracy r| additive s.d. (sim. units)| predicted response (sim. units)| realised response (sim. units)| |-----------:|----------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------------:|------------------------------:| | 1.774| 0.702| 4.742| 5.908| 5.116|
::: ::: In this single draw (seed 1) the equation overpredicts, by about 13 percent. @tbl-response-gap splits that gap into the intensity and the regression parts. ::: {#tbl-response-gap .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The gap of @tbl-response-breeders split into intensity and regression parts (same draw, seed 1). Intensities: normal-theory value of the selected fraction and realised standardised selection differential on the index. Responses: @eq-response-breeders with the realised intensity; the regression of genetic value on the index times the selection differential; the realised response. Last column: skewness of the standardised index. Responses in simulation units.'} ```{.r .cell-code} i_real <- (mean(I[sel]) - mean(I)) / sd(I) b <- cov(gv, I) / var(I) # regression of value on criterion fmt(data.frame( `intensity, normal theory` = i_norm, `intensity, realised` = i_real, `response with realised intensity (sim. units)` = i_real * r * sd(gv), `response from regression (sim. units)` = b * (mean(I[sel]) - mean(I)), `realised response (sim. units)` = mean(gv[sel]) - mean(gv), `index skewness` = mean(scale(I)^3), check.names = FALSE), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| intensity, normal theory| intensity, realised| response with realised intensity (sim. units)| response from regression (sim. units)| realised response (sim. units)| index skewness| |------------------------:|-------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------:|------------------------------:|--------------:| | 1.774| 1.701| 5.662| 5.662| 5.116| -0.17|
::: ::: Two identities can be read off it. The response from regression and the response with realised intensity are the same quantity written twice, since $b\,S_I = i\,r\,\sigma_A$ identically, with $S_I$ the selection differential on the index. The chunk below asserts it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(b * (mean(I[sel]) - mean(I)), i_real * r * sd(gv)))) ``` ::: With $N =$ 625 candidates and $n =$ 60 selected, $i = \varphi(z)/(n/N)$, with $z$ the standard-normal truncation point that leaves a fraction $n/N$ above it and $\varphi$ the standard-normal density, is the intensity of an infinitely large normal population [@falconer1996, ch. 11]. At this finite $N$ the expected standardised mean of the top $n$ of $N$ independent normal draws is smaller. A single draw cannot tell whether the remaining gap is structural or sampling, so @tbl-response-replicated repeats the same `simulate_pools()` call over 30 seeds, and the finite-$N$ intensity is estimated from 4000 normal samples. ::: {#tbl-response-replicated .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The single draw of @tbl-response-breeders repeated over seeds 1 to 30 of the same `simulate_pools()` call (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, 300 QTL, $h^2 = 0.5$, $F_{ST} = 0.15$; top 60 of 625 hybrids on the index). Per quantity: mean over seeds, standard error of that mean (s.d./$\sqrt{30}$), minimum and maximum. Relative gap: $1 -$ realised/predicted response (@eq-response-breeders), dimensionless; realised intensity: standardised selection differential on the index; skewness of the standardised index.'} ```{.r .cell-code} one_seed <- function(s) { sm <- simulate_pools(n_A = book_cfg$n_pool_A, n_B = book_cfg$n_pool_B, m = book_cfg$m, fst = 0.15, n_qtl = 300, h2 = 0.5, seed = s) g <- drop(sm$X %*% sm$beta) Ix <- sm$index top <- order(Ix, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)] pred <- sel_intensity(n_sel / length(Ix)) * cor(Ix, g) * sd(g) c(rel_gap = 1 - (mean(g[top]) - mean(g)) / pred, i_real = (mean(Ix[top]) - mean(Ix)) / sd(Ix), skew = mean(scale(Ix)^3)) } rep_seeds <- t(vapply(1:30, one_seed, numeric(3))) gap_se <- sd(rep_seeds[, "rel_gap"]) / sqrt(nrow(rep_seeds)) stopifnot(abs(mean(rep_seeds[, "rel_gap"])) < 2 * gap_se) # the claim below set.seed(11) i_finite <- replicate(4000, { z <- rnorm(N) (mean(sort(z, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)]) - mean(z)) / sd(z) }) fmt(data.frame( quantity = c("relative gap 1 - realised/predicted", "realised intensity", "index skewness"), `mean over seeds` = colMeans(rep_seeds), `s.e.` = apply(rep_seeds, 2, sd) / sqrt(nrow(rep_seeds)), minimum = apply(rep_seeds, 2, min), maximum = apply(rep_seeds, 2, max), row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|quantity | mean over seeds| s.e.| minimum| maximum| |:-----------------------------------|---------------:|-----:|-------:|-------:| |relative gap 1 - realised/predicted | 0.006| 0.016| -0.211| 0.134| |realised intensity | 1.776| 0.010| 1.677| 1.883| |index skewness | -0.001| 0.024| -0.292| 0.241|
::: ::: Over the 30 seeds the mean relative gap is 0.006 (standard error 0.016), the prediction exceeds the realised response in 19 of 30 seeds, and the mean realised intensity is 1.776 against a finite-$N$ normal expectation of 1.771 (s.d. 0.044) and the infinite-population value 1.774. The replicated mean gap is within two standard errors of zero, so at this scale the seed-1 overprediction is consistent with sampling variation, and the equation shows no detectable bias; the replicated AlphaSimR sweep of @sec-alphasimr reaches the same reading. One limit applies: only the teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, $F_{ST} = 0.15$) was measured, so nothing here says how the gap behaves at production scale or under selection across cycles. ## Genic variance, and what it has to do with gene diversity The additive variance in @eq-response-breeders is not a fixed property of the population. Split it in two. **Genic variance** is what the loci would contribute if they were independent: $$V_{\text{genic}} \;=\; \sum_k \beta_k^2 \operatorname{Var}(x_k)$$ {#eq-response-genic} with $\beta_k$ the effect of marker $k$ and $x_k$ its hybrid genotype. **Realised variance** is what the population actually has, $\operatorname{Var} (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)$, which is the sum of the *whole* covariance matrix rather than only its diagonal. The difference is exactly the gametic-phase disequilibrium term [@bulmer1971], which @tbl-response-genic evaluates for the seed-1 draw: $$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) - V_{\text{genic}} \;=\; 2\sum_{k |quantity | value (sim. units squared)| |:---------------------|--------------------------:| |realised variance | 22.4837| |genic variance | 25.2051| |disequilibrium term | -2.7214| |deviation from oracle | 0.0000| ::: ::: How does $V_{\text{genic}}$ relate to gene diversity? Let $p_{Ak}$ and $p_{Bk}$ be the frequencies of the allele coded 1 at locus $k$ among the inbred lines of pools A and B, $q = 1 - p$, and $p_k = (p_{Ak} + p_{Bk})/2$ the hybrid-pool frequency. A hybrid of the complete A $\times$ B factorial carries $x_k = (u_k + v_k)/2$, with $u_k \in \{0, 1\}$ the allele of its pool-A parent and $v_k \in \{0, 1\}$ that of its pool-B parent (the $u_{ik}$, $v_{jk}$ of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca without the line index), drawn independently from the two pools, so over the factorial (population-variance scale) $$\operatorname{Var}(x_k) \;=\; \frac{p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk}}{4} \;=\; \frac{p_k q_k}{2} - \frac{(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2}{8}.$$ {#eq-response-hybrid-var} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pA <- colMeans(sim$GL[sim$pool == "A", ]) pB <- colMeans(sim$GL[sim$pool == "B", ]) pH <- (pA + pB) / 2 v_pop <- colMeans(X^2) - colMeans(X)^2 stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(v_pop, (pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB)) / 4)), isTRUE(all.equal(v_pop, pH * (1 - pH) / 2 - (pA - pB)^2 / 8))) ok <- pH > 0 & pH < 1 c(ratio_min = min(v_pop[ok] / (pH * (1 - pH))[ok]), ratio_max = max(v_pop[ok] / (pH * (1 - pH))[ok])) ``` ::: The per-locus variance entering $V_{\text{genic}}$ (@eq-response-genic) is therefore not proportional to $p_k q_k$: the ratio $\operatorname{Var}(x_k)/(p_k q_k)$ ranges from 0.107 to 0.5 across these loci. Gene diversity of the hybrid pool, $\frac{1}{m}\sum_k 2 p_k q_k$, contains the between-pool divergence $(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2$ that @eq-response-hybrid-var subtracts (since $2p_kq_k = p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk} + (p_{Ak} - p_{Bk})^2/2$), the between-pool term of the partition of @sec-subdivided, while $V_{\text{genic}}$ among hybrids sees only the within-pool part, weighted by squared effect. The inference is that gene diversity is a proxy for genic variance only through its within-pool part, and only if effect sizes are unrelated to which loci lose diversity; this chapter does not test the second condition. The proxy is incomplete in two further ways. Gene diversity weights every locus equally, so it cannot distinguish a marker carrying half the genetic variance from one carrying none. And -- more seriously -- ::: {.callout-warning} ## The frequency-based metrics cannot see the disequilibrium term $\theta$, $GD$, $N_s$, allelic richness, `F_hom` and `F_drift` -- including $\theta$, the only metric the differential evolution (DE) selector constrains -- are all functions of allele frequencies **one locus at a time**. The covariance term of @eq-response-ld does not move a single allele frequency. `eff_dim()` is the exception: it is computed from the spectrum of the double-centred $f$, a multilocus quantity, so it does respond to disequilibrium, but it weights loci by nothing, not by effect. A flat gene diversity trajectory therefore does not imply flat additive variance: reading it as one puts the error of @eq-response-ld, the whole disequilibrium term, into $\sigma_A^2$ and from there into the predicted $R$ of @eq-response-breeders. @sec-limits measures how far apart the two can travel. ::: ## Combining ability as the additive part Additive variance is the variance of *breeding values*, not of genotypic values, and in a two-pool hybrid population the average effect of an allele substitution depends on which pool it is substituted into. The exact orthogonal split of a hybrid value into general and specific combining ability (GCA, SCA) [@sprague1942] is developed in @sec-heterosis-gca-sca, a later chapter; it is used here ahead of that derivation: each line's GCA is its average effect against the opposite pool, i.e. the additive part *relative to that tester pool*, never a property of the line alone. The chunk below applies it to an illustrative, dominance-only value $H$ = `heterosis_value(X, d)`, with deviations $d_k \sim N(0.3, 0.1^2)$ drawn here and unrelated to $\boldsymbol\beta$. Its shares are shares of that illustrative heterosis, not of the genetic variance of `gv`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(7) d <- rnorm(ncol(X), 0.3, 0.1) # dominance deviations U <- sim$GL[sim$pool == "A", ] V <- sim$GL[sim$pool == "B", ] gs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d) H <- heterosis_value(X, d) nA <- nrow(U); nB <- nrow(V) gA <- rep(gs$gca_A, times = nB) # ped varies pool A fastest gB <- rep(gs$gca_B, each = nA) sc <- as.vector(gs$sca) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(H, gs$mu + gA + gB + sc)), isTRUE(all.equal(var(H), var(gA) + var(gB) + var(sc))), max(abs(c(cov(gA, gB), cov(gA, sc), cov(gB, sc)))) < 1e-10) c(reconstruction_dev = max(abs(H - (gs$mu + gA + gB + sc))), var_H = var(H), sum_of_components = var(gA) + var(gB) + var(sc), identity_dev = abs(var(H) - (var(gA) + var(gB) + var(sc)))) ``` ::: The three components are orthogonal, so their variances add exactly. @tbl-response-gca-sca gives the shares. ::: {#tbl-response-gca-sca .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Variance of the illustrative dominance-only value $H$ = `heterosis_value(X, d)` (dominance deviations $d_k \sim N(0.3, 0.1^2)$, seed 7; one draw, 25 $\times$ 25 factorial of the seed-1 pools) split into the general combining ability of pool A and pool B lines and the specific combining ability of their crosses. Variance in simulation units; share of the sum. These are shares of the illustrative heterosis, not of the genetic variance of the selected trait.'} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- c(gca_A = var(gA), gca_B = var(gB), sca = var(sc)) fmt(data.frame(component = names(p), variance = p, share = p / sum(p)), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| |component | variance| share| |:-----|:---------|--------:|-----:| |gca_A |gca_A | 9.064| 0.238| |gca_B |gca_B | 8.673| 0.228| |sca |sca | 20.376| 0.535|
::: ::: `gca_A` and `gca_B` are the part of $H$ that main effects of the parent lines, each against the opposite pool, can express; `sca` is the line-by-line interaction they cannot. How each share responds to recurrent selection across cycles is not measured in this chapter. ## What `weights = NULL` is assuming `stage2_select()` defaults (`weights = NULL`) to equal weight on every trait, and every chapter of this book including @sec-case-study takes that default. The criteria it weights are not phenotypes but the *predicted* trait values $\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ of the hybrids (`hybrids` columns, passed to `build_ctx()` as `traits`). `build_ctx()` standardises each column before weighting, so the default index is $\sum_j \hat g_j / \operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)$, up to a positive affine transformation that does not change the ranking. In trait units that is the index $\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ with economic weights $a_j = 1/\operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)$. What the default assumes is therefore an economic statement: one standard deviation of predicted value is worth the same in every trait. It is a choice, not a neutral one. Whether $\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is the best index for those $\mathbf{a}$ is a separate question, and the answer depends on what $\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is. Let $W = \mathbf{a}'\mathbf{g}$ be the aggregate genotype (the breeding objective), with $\mathbf{g}$ the vector of the traits' genetic values (one entry per trait; not a vector over individuals). The weights $\mathbf{b}$ on a vector of criteria $\mathbf{c}$ that maximise the correlation between $\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{c}$ and $W$ are $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{c})^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{g}')\,\mathbf{a}$. When $\mathbf{c} = \hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is the multi-trait best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of $\mathbf{g}$, $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{g}}, \mathbf{g}') = \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\mathbf{g}})$, so $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a}$: weighting the predictions by the economic weights is then the optimum, not a departure from it. The condition fails in general for predictions that are not BLUP of $\mathbf{g}$, single-trait BLUPs of genetically correlated traits included. When $\mathbf{c}$ is instead the vector of phenotypic records $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g} + \mathbf{e}$, $\mathbf{e}$ independent of $\mathbf{g}$, with $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{y}) = \boldsymbol\Sigma_P$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{g}') = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G$, the same expression is the Smith-Hazel index [@smith1936; @hazel1943]: $$\mathbf{b} \;=\; \boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a},$$ {#eq-response-smith-hazel} with $\boldsymbol\Sigma_P$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma_G$ the phenotypic and genetic covariance matrices of the traits (`P` and `G` in the code; $\boldsymbol\Sigma_G$ is not the relationship matrix $\mathbf{G}$) and $\mathbf{a}$ the economic weights. @tbl-response-smith-hazel evaluates @eq-response-smith-hazel for a two-trait example. ::: {#tbl-response-smith-hazel .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Smith-Hazel index weights (@eq-response-smith-hazel) for an illustrative two-trait example with equal economic weights. Phenotypic covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_P$: variances 4.0 and 1.0, covariance 1.2; genetic covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_G$: variances 2.0 and 0.3, covariance 0.3. Values are invented for illustration, not estimated.'} ```{.r .cell-code} P <- matrix(c(4.0, 1.2, 1.2, 1.0), 2) # phenotypic covariance G <- matrix(c(2.0, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3), 2) # genetic covariance a <- c(1, 1) # equal economic weight stopifnot(all(eigen(G, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0), # G is a covariance all(eigen(P - G, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0)) # so is P - G fmt(data.frame(trait = c("yield", "moisture"), `economic weight` = a, `Smith-Hazel weight` = index_smith_hazel(P, G, a), check.names = FALSE), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|trait | economic weight| Smith-Hazel weight| |:--------|---------------:|------------------:| |yield | 1| 0.617| |moisture | 1| -0.141|
::: ::: Equal economic weights do **not** give equal index weights on phenotypes here. $\mathbf{b}$ is proportional to $\mathbf{a}$ if and only if $\mathbf{a}$ is an eigenvector of $\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_G$. A sufficient condition is $\boldsymbol\Sigma_G = c\,\boldsymbol\Sigma_P$ -- every trait with heritability $c$ and genetic correlations equal to the phenotypic ones -- which requires neither equal variances nor uncorrelated traits. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(index_smith_hazel(P, 0.5 * P, a), 0.5 * a))) # BLUP of g from one record per trait (known means): ghat = G P^-1 y. K <- G %*% solve(P) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(drop(solve(K %*% P %*% t(K), K %*% G) %*% a), a)), isTRUE(all.equal(drop(t(K) %*% a), index_smith_hazel(P, G, a)))) ``` ::: The chunk also checks the two statements that tie the phenotypic and the predicted index together, for the BLUP from one record per trait with known means, $\hat{\mathbf{g}} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\mathbf{y}$: $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\mathbf{g}})^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{g}}, \mathbf{g}')\,\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}$, and $\mathbf{a}'\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is the Smith-Hazel index $\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{y}$ of @tbl-response-smith-hazel. So the gap between $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{a}$ in that table is a property of an index on phenotypes; it is not a defect of `weights = NULL`, whose criteria are predictions. What the default does assume is the economic weighting $a_j = 1/\operatorname{sd}(\hat g_j)$, and that the predictions behave as multi-trait BLUP; this chapter tests neither against a real breeding objective. ## The $\alpha$ constraint is a restricted index @sec-ocs will argue that a diversity *budget* is approvable where a weighted sum is not: "I accept losing five percent" is a sentence a breeding committee can sign, and "diversity is worth $\lambda$ index units" is not. That argument is usually presented as a point about human decision-making. It is older and harder than that. @kempthorne1959 posed exactly the same problem -- maximise aggregate gain subject to **zero expected change** in a specified direction -- and solved it. In the $\mathbf{C} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{R}$ form used by `index_restricted()` (algebraically equivalent; not necessarily their notation), with $\mathbf{R}$ the $n_t \times n_r$ matrix of restricted directions for $n_t$ traits and $n_r$ restrictions: $$\mathbf{b} \;=\; \boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{C} (\mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1}\mathbf{C})^{-1}\mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol\Sigma_P^{-1} \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{a}\right], \qquad \mathbf{C} = \boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{R}$$ {#eq-response-restricted} @tbl-response-restricted compares it with the unrestricted index of @tbl-response-smith-hazel when moisture is held at zero gain. ::: {#tbl-response-restricted .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Unrestricted (Smith-Hazel, @eq-response-smith-hazel) and restricted (@eq-response-restricted) index weights for the two-trait example of @tbl-response-smith-hazel, with the restriction holding moisture at zero expected gain ($\mathbf{R} = (0, 1)\'$). Last column: expected gain in the restricted trait, $\mathbf{R}\'\boldsymbol\Sigma_G\mathbf{b}$, in trait units.'} ```{.r .cell-code} R <- cbind(c(0, 1)) # hold moisture at zero gain b_r <- index_restricted(P, G, a, R) b_u <- index_smith_hazel(P, G, a) fmt(data.frame( index = c("Smith-Hazel", "restricted"), `weight on yield` = c(b_u[1], b_r[1]), `weight on moisture` = c(b_u[2], b_r[2]), `expected gain in moisture (trait units)` = c(drop(crossprod(R, G %*% b_u)), drop(crossprod(R, G %*% b_r))), check.names = FALSE), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|index | weight on yield| weight on moisture| expected gain in moisture (trait units)| |:-----------|---------------:|------------------:|---------------------------------------:| |Smith-Hazel | 0.6172| -0.1406| 0.143| |restricted | 0.6538| -0.6538| 0.000|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(max(abs(crossprod(R, G %*% b_r))) < 1e-12) ``` ::: The restricted index moves the restricted trait by exactly zero -- not approximately, not on average. That is the property distinguishing a restriction from a penalty, and it is the property $\alpha$ inherits. ::: {.callout-important} ## What is genuinely new in this book, then Not the idea of constraining rather than pricing: that is 1959. What is new is the restricted direction. @kempthorne1959 restricted a *trait*. This book restricts the loss of molecular gene diversity, which is not a trait, has no economic weight, and is measured on a matrix rather than a phenotype. The algebra of restriction carries over; the object being restricted does not. Stating the lineage makes @sec-ocs stronger, not weaker. A theorem from 1959 stands behind the move. ::: ## Where this connects @sec-genomic-era and @sec-catalogue measure the allele frequencies from which, through @eq-response-hybrid-var, the genic variance defined here is built; the link to variance runs through the within-pool part only. @sec-genomic-prediction measures the $r$ this chapter took as given, and Finding 5 of @sec-choosing shows what happens when it is assumed rather than measured. @sec-ocs is where the restricted index becomes the $\alpha$ constraint, and @sec-limits is where the disequilibrium term this chapter isolated (@eq-response-ld) turns out to matter more than @eq-response-breeders suggests. ## Reproduce this chapter {.unnumbered} All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: [**02b-response.R**](https://ederdbs.github.io/QG/downloads/02b-response.R){download="02b-response.R"}. Download it, install `hybdiv`, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.
